schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the unusual 'they made king' as a hint of a disputed succession, with only Athaliah able to contest it; Ellicott takes the fuller notice, and the 'band of Arabians' who slew the captive princes, as marks of a different source.
Gill notes Ahaziah was the sole surviving son, spared when the rest were slain (cf. 2 Chron. 21:17).
Clarke says the elder sons were slain by the Arabians and sketches the whole arc of the wicked reign.
Henry frames the reign as the ruin worked by ungodly counsel and Athaliah's war on David's house, against which no word of God shall fall.

debates.question: Why does the accession use the unusual formula, 'the inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah king'?

sides.position: It hints at a disputed or doubtful succession
It simply reflects the chronicler's use of a different source

themes: the youngest and sole surviving son

schools.summary: Clarke calls 'forty-two' impossible (it would make the son older than his father) and a mem-for-caph slip; Wesley adds the manuscript witnesses, including the ancient Antioch Syriac, for the true reading twenty-two.

Keil and Delitzsch call it an orthographic error (beth for mem), the son no older than twenty-two; Ellicott confirms the transcription error and notes Athaliah is granddaughter of Omri, the chronicler dropping Kings' 'king of Israel.'
Gill holds twenty-two undoubtedly correct.
Henry inclines to a transcriber's slip but records the alternative that 'forty-two' is Athaliah's age, put for her son's in reproach.

debates.question: How is 'forty-two years old' to be explained?

sides.position: A scribal error for 'twenty-two,' as the versions read
'Son of forty-two years' means the age of his mother Athaliah, put for his in reproach

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the emphatic 'he too' and the chronicler's added clause about the mother, whose influence backed the Baal-worship that symbolized alliance with the north; Keil grounds the sin in the tutelage of Jezebel's daughter.
Clarke paints Athaliah as wicked daughter, wicked spouse, every relation a channel of corruption.
Gill binds the son's course to his father Jehoram's.

Keil notes the chronicler adds that Ahab's kin became Ahaziah's counsellors 'to his destruction' (cf. 2 Chron. 20:23), leading him into the fatal war; Ellicott reads the whole clause as the chronicler's own expansion of Kings' 'son-in-law of the house of Ahab.'
Wesley notes that while the father lived he seduced his son himself; only after his death did Ahab's house take over the tutelage.
Gill refers back to the verdict already passed on the house of Ahab.

Ellicott hears an echo of Ps. 1:1, notes the chronicler's added 'king of Israel' and 'against Hazael,' and the curious 'ha-rammim' the LXX read as 'the archers'; Keil explains the chronicler suppresses Jehu's conspiracy as outside his plan.
Clarke refers to the fuller account at 2 Kings 8:28.
Gill: Ahaziah did just as his counsellors advised, in state as in religion.

Keil and Ellicott dwell on the unique word 'tebusah' (downtreading, found only here) and read the coincidence of the visit with Jehu's revolt as providence, sweeping Joram, Jezebel, and Ahaziah into one ruin while Athaliah escaped.
Gill: the destruction was of God's appointing, an overruling providence ordering the occasion justly for the king's sins.

themes: the house of Ahab in one ruin

schools.summary: Keil records the killing as proof of the divinely directed extirpation of Ahab's house (details at 2 Kings 10:12-14); Ellicott presses 'executing judgment' as a legal 'pleading' (cf. 1 Sam 12:7; Joel 3:2), Jehu an instrument of vengeance like the Assyrian of Isa 10:5-7, and takes the forty-two as kinsmen in the wide sense.
Gill sets the slaughter within Jehu's wider carnage of Joram and seventy kinsfolk, courtiers, and priests.

debates.question: Who were the 'sons of the brethren of Ahaziah' whom Jehu slew?

sides.position: Kinsmen in the wide sense — nephews, cousins, grandsons, forty-two in number
Ahaziah's own literal brothers, the chronicler having invented the earlier massacre

themes: Jehu as instrument of divine vengeance

schools.summary: Keil holds the divergent 2 Kings 9:27 account (death at Megiddo) reconcilable with this; Ellicott instead welcomes the divergence as proof of two independent traditions, and marks the burial-for-Jehoshaphat's-sake and the closing clause as the chronicler's own style (cf. 2 Chron. 13:20).
Clarke points to the different account at 2 Kings 9:27 as one to be reconciled; Wesley notes the wounded king had escaped.
Gill: Ahaziah fled when Joram was wounded by Jehu.

debates.question: How do the two accounts of Ahaziah's death relate?

sides.position: Divergent details of one event, to be reconciled
Two independent traditions whose very divergence is valuable

themes: no strength left for the kingdom

schools.summary: Keil notes Athaliah's massacre of all the royal house but the rescued infant Joash (cf. 2 Kings 11:1-3); Ellicott corrects the Hebrew 'she spake' to 'destroyed' and notes the seed royal included kin beyond Ahaziah's offspring left after vv.1, 8.
Henry frames a wicked woman destroying David's house to seat her own family, against a good woman about to preserve the lamp of God's anointed.
Clarke: the Messianic promise hung on the brittle thread of one infant's life, kept whole by miraculous providence against earth and hell.

themes: Athaliah's massacre of the seed royal
the wicked woman against David's house
the Messianic line on a thread

schools.summary: Keil identifies Jehoshabeath as Jehoram's daughter, Jehoiada's wife, and Ahaziah's sister; Ellicott glosses the name (cf. Exod 6:23; Luke 1:7), 'that were to be put to death,' and the 'chamber of beds' (2 Kings 11:2), and defends the historicity of the priest's marriage with Josephus and Ewald against Thenius.
Henry: a good woman preserving the house of David, that a lamp might be ordained for God's anointed.

debates.question: Was Jehoshabeath the wife of Jehoiada, the child hidden in the temple?

sides.position: To be doubted, since the high priest did not live in the temple

themes: the king's daughter and the priest's wife
the good woman preserving the line

schools.summary: Clarke, with the Targum, places the child in the sanctuary — the holy of holies — beyond Athaliah's reach, hidden with his aunt through her whole reign.
Ellicott notes the 'with them / with her / with him' variants for the child's keepers (cf. 2 Kings 11:3); Keil reads the six years of concealment set against Athaliah's usurped reign.
Henry: the child preserved that a lamp might be ordained for God's anointed — the Messianic promise kept whole against earth and hell.

themes: hidden in the house of God

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the text ('and he'=Joram; 'of the wounds' not 'because'; makkim only at 2 Kings 8:29; 9:15) and calls 'Azariah' a slip for 'Ahaziah'; Keil reads the visit to the sick Joram as the providential step to Ahaziah's destruction.
Clarke lets Jehoahaz, Ahaziah, and Azariah stand as three genuine names of the one king.
Henry: Ahaziah's courtesy visit to Joram brought him, as in a snare, to the moment of Jehu's judgment.

debates.question: Is 'Azariah' in this verse a genuine name of the king or a scribal error?

sides.position: A copyist's slip for 'Ahaziah,' the reading of the versions
A genuine name, the king bearing Jehoahaz, Ahaziah, and Azariah alike
